newsitem.title: USA: U.S. T-bond up, weathers jump in jobs, eyes wage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. T-bond up, weathers jump in jobs, eyes wage.

text.p: U.S. Treasury bond prices wiped out a near one-point loss to trade higher early Friday, shrugging off a sharp rise in February jobs growth and focusing instead on timid wage inflation, traders said.

Bond prices initially fell on the strength of the overall number, but as analysts studied the components, it quickly became apparent there were no threatening inflationary indicators in the statistics.
U.S. Treasury securities have since rebounded into positive territory.

"The wage component was very helpful, but I'm not sure it's enough to hold (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan off. He's already spoken about being preemptive and I'm not sure how good you should feel about (a very strong number)," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.

The Labor Department reported that February witnessed the creation of 339,000 jobs, stronger than average forecasts of 230,000 new jobs. But, earnings rose by only three cents an hour, meaning wage inflation remained in check.
The bond market's positive reaction to the payrolls figure was somewhat mysterious to John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co.
"The quit rate -- the statistic du jour -- edges down, but the interesting fact is that the fundamental story is the U.S. economy is growing at a very strong pace," Williams said.
The voluntary job leavers, or "quit rate," fell to 10.9 percent from 12.3 percent the prior month.
Williams said he raised his first quarter Gross Domestic Product growth estimate to 3.0 percent based on the rise in the work week. Average weekly hours jumped to 35.0 from 34.2.
"A lot of people are working a lot of hours and they must be making a lot of stuff," Williams said.
